News.title: Three people injured after police chase ends in horror two car crash on busy road in Bradford
News.content:
POLICE CHASE SMASH Three people injured after police chase ends in horror two car crash on busy road in Bradford

Credit: Facebook/G2K

THREE men have been injured after a police chase on a busy city road ended in a horror smash.

Emergency services rushed to the scene of the collision where two men had to be rescued after being left trapped in their cars.



The horror smash occurred just past midnight in the early hours of Saturday morning in Bradford.



Cops said a Volkswagen Golf had failed to stop for police.

Trying to flee, the hatchback immediately collided with a Skoda.

Photographs from the scene show at least one car sat in the road with a crumpled bonnet and debris scattered across the road.

The crash was so severe that one man from each car was trapped and had to be freed by the fire service.



A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said: “Two cars were involved with one person trapped in each vehicle.

“An extrication was carried out by fire service personnel and casualties transferred to hospital by ambulance.

“Two appliances from Bradford attended.”

The driver of the Skoda is being treated in hospital for a leg injury.



Two men from the Golf were also hospitalised with non-life threatening injuries.

West Yorkshire Police said: “At 12.23am this morning (April 11) a vehicle failed to stop for police on Leeds Road in Bradford.

“The vehicle, a Golf, was then immediately involved in a road collision with a Skoda.

“Two men in the Golf were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and the man in the Skoda was treated in hospital for a leg injury.

“Enquiries remain ongoing by the Roads Policing Unit.”

News.title: One dead and several injured after ‘multiple masked gunmen’ open fire at a Chick-fil-A as witnesses describe ‘warzone’
News.content:
FATAL SHOOTING One dead and several injured after ‘multiple masked gunmen’ open fire at a Chick-fil-A as witnesses describe ‘warzone’

ONE person has been killed and several injured after a mass shooting at a popular fast food restaurant.

At least six people were shot at a Chick-fil-A in New Jersey last night when several masked and armed suspects allegedly burst into the branch and opened fire.





Terror reigned at the restaurant in Union Township as witnesses said shooters opened fire on terrified customers and staff.

The branch was locked down with workers still inside, reports said.

A man who said his girlfriend worked at the location said the masked men charged into the restaurant, forced their way behind the counter and fired multiple shots.

The dad of a Chick-fil-A worker said the restaurant became a “warzone” as the suspected shooters stormed the store.



He said several of his son’s co-workers had been injured.

More than seven shots were fired, according to a taxi driver who was dropping off a customer nearby.

He told ABC: “I finished my trip over there, in the return zone.

“I heard the shots. When I finished the trip, I go to Chick-fil-A to buy two burgers – I see the police, I heard the shots very close.”



Prosecutor’s spokeswoman Lauren Farinas said officials are conducting “an active and ongoing investigation”.

She added: “More information will be released as it becomes available.”

Former New Jersey Assemblyman Jamel Holley said: “Numerous people are injured & one confirmed dead as emergency crews are on the scene responding to a mass shooting after gunfire erupted inside a Chick-fil-A in Union, New Jersey.

“Keep everyone in your prayers.”

News.title: At least 30 dead in horror stampede at popular tourist hotspot with ‘many young people’ feared to be among victims
News.content:
AT LEAST 30 people have been killed in a horror stampede at a holiday hotspot in the Caribbean, with many students feared to be among the dead.

The fatal crush happened at packed tourist attraction, Laferriere Citadel in northern Haiti.



Haiti‘s PM Alix Didier Fils-Aime confirmed “many young people” were visiting the tourist site when the tragedy unfolded.



He gave “sincere condolences to the bereaved families” and “assures them of his profound solidarity during this time of mourning and great suffering”.

Revellers had gathered for a celebration at the UNESCO world heritage site when chaos broke out.

Emergency services rushed to the scene but there was little that could be done to save many of the victims.

At least 30 people were killed – but authorities warned that the death toll is likely to rise as many remain missing.



A desperate search and rescue mission is underway to find any more survivors.

Several dozen people have been injured and were rushed to nearby hospitals.

Local official Jean Henri Petit said the deadly stampede happened at the entrance to the site, and was worsened by rain.

There was an unexpectedly large number of visitors to the site, Le Nouvelliste reported.



The paper said panic broke out after tourists were forced through a single entrance and exit point.

Shocking video showed terrified young people trapped in the crush at the overcrowded site.

An investigation into the tragedy has been launched.

The Caribbean nation’s capital Port-au-Prince has branded the world’s most dangerous city, plagued by 200 gangs that rule its streets.

It comes as 39 people were crushed to death in a horror stampede at a political rally last year.



A stampede crushed multiple people after large crowds gathered in support of Tamil actor and politician Vijay in southern India.

Among the dead were at least six children and 16 women, according to the Tamil Nadu Health Minister Ma Subramanian.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Vijay, a candidate for the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam party, was in the region on one stage of an ongoing state tour.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the ordeal was “deeply saddening” in a public statement to social media platform X.

News.title: Boy, 15, shot in Birmingham park as cops launch manhunt for gunman & appeal for CCTV
News.content:
SHOOTING HORROR Boy, 15, shot in Birmingham park as cops launch manhunt for gunman & appeal for CCTV

A 15-YEAR-OLD boy was rushed to hospital after being shot in a park – with police launching a manhunt for the gunman.

Paramedics were called to Ward End Park in Birmingham just before 10pm on Friday (April 10).





Armed officers are understood to have been scrambled to the scene and initially gave the boy first aid.

The teenager – found near the Foxton Road entrance – was taken to hospital with gunshot wounds, where he remains in a stable condition, according to West Midlands Police.

His injuries are not believed to be life threatening.



Our Major Crime Unit (MCU) is investigating, including the review of CCTV in and around the park.

Detective Superintendent Ryan Chambers, from our MCU, said: “This appears to be an isolated incident and there will be an increased police presence in the area to assist with the investigation and reassure the community.”

We are appealing to anyone who was in the area or may have witnessed the incident, to get in touch with us.

You can do so via Live Chat on our website or by calling 101 quoting log 5589 of April 10.

News.title: US and Iran FAIL to agree peace deal as talks break down after 21 hours in Pakistan leaving fragile ceasefire on brink
News.content:
JD VANCE has blasted Iran for refusing to accept Donald Trump’s “simple proposal” for peace after 21 hours of crunch talks failed.

The vice president said he offered the regime a final and best offer but they refused, as both delegations quickly left Pakistan empty handed in the early hours of Sunday morning.





Vance – who led the US delegation – added: “So we go back to the United States, having not come to an agreement.”

The main sticking point during the lengthy talks came due to Iran’s refusal to halt their nuclear ambitions, the US said.

Vance told reporters as he boarded Air Force Two to leave Islamabad: “Do we see a fundamental commitment of will for the Iranians not to develop a nuclear weapon… for the long term?



“We haven’t seen that yet.”

American negotiators insisted they were flexible and accommodating across the peace attempts.

A Pakistani source said there were “mood swings” from both sides with the temperature shifting “up and down” throughout the meeting.

There remains slim hope of the fragile ceasefire currently in place extending.



Vance concluded: “We leave here with a very simple proposal; a method of understanding that is our final and best offer.

“We’ll see if the Iranians accept it.”

Iranian negotiators left Pakistan shortly after Vance announced the failed talks.

Iran’s foreign ministry said the talks were conducted in an atmosphere of “mistrust”, and called on Washington to refrain from “excessive demands and unlawful requests”.



The regime blamed the US for collapsing negotiations.

Fars News Agency quoted one source as saying: “The Americans demanded through negotiations everything they could not obtain through war.”

They added that the main disagreements came over nuclear technology and the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked off by Iran since the start of the conflict.

A source close to the negotiators believed “the American team was looking for an excuse to leave the negotiating table”.

Israel have weighed in on the discussion with security cabinet minister Zeev Elkin saying more talks are still an option, but warned: “The Iranians are playing with fire.”



The two-week ceasefire agreed on Tuesday began after Trump vowed to unleash a “civilisation-ending blitz” on Iran if the regime refused terms to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

It remains unclear if attacks on Iran will resume while a reopening of the vital waterway now appears to be off the table.

It comes after US officials revealed the withering regime has stalled reopening the vital shipping lane because it cannot locate the mines it planted.



As Vance left Pakistan with no deal, Trump was spotted in Miami watching a UFC cage fight.

It was unclear whether the US president knew negotiations had failed by the time he entered the arena for the event.

But Vance said he had spoken to the US president several times during the course of the discussions.

On his way to Florida Trump had told reporters it did not matter to him if a deal was reached.

“We win regardless”, he said. Adding: “We’ve defeated them militarily.”



On Saturday, Trump declared he is now “clearing out” the Strait of Hormuz to allow for global trade to pass through the key waterway again.

The US president said the heavily-mined strait would be safe to pass again soon as in a show of strength he ordered two US Navy destroyers to travel across through the vital shipping lane as the make-or-break summit began.

The risky move – the first time US warships have crossed the strait since the start of the six-week war – was reportedly carried out without Iran’s knowledge.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tehran later called it a violation of the fragile two-week ceasefire deal.

A US official said the bold move was designed to encourage the globe that ships can begin to pass the commercial shipping and break Iran’s iron grip on the route.

News.title: Labour urged to tackle crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs
News.content:
LABOUR is being urged to tackle the crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs.

Tax rises are making it hard for firms to employ them, according to MPs.





Higher minimum wages, National Insurance hikes and employment rights changes are hitting businesses.

The number of NEETs — young people not in education, employment or training — is close to a million.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Builders are desperate to hire [young people] but Labour have piled on costs that make it too expensive to give them a chance.

“You don’t fix youth unemployment by taxing the jobs they need. If we want our kids earning, we’ve got to cut the costs and stop pricing young people out of work.”



Reform’s Lee Anderson said: “All Labour has been successful at is destroying the job market while young people struggle to get a foot on the ladder.”

The Sun on Sunday’s Builder Better Britain campaign has helped secure youngsters placements in construction trades.

A Government spokesman said: “This Government inherited a dire shortage of construction workers and is determined to deliver more opportunities.

“That’s why our youth employment support package, totalling £2.5billion, includes the offer of £2,000 for each new employee aged 16 to 24 taken on by a small business, supporting almost one million young people and delivering up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn.”



They said those hiring under-21s earning below a certain level do not pay NI contributions.

News.title: Britain is at its weakest in 400 years – we need to prioritise bullets over benefits, Kemi Badenoch warns Starmer
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has warned Britain is at its weakest in 400 years — as she pledged to go on the biggest ever peacetime rearming blitz.

The Tory leader said the UK has been “prioritising benefits over bullets” and is facing a day of reckoning.





Unleashing both ­barrels on PM Sir Keir Starmer, she branded his failure to find the billions needed to fund our military “a national disgrace”.

And she accused the Government of lying by ­pretending we are prepared for war, adding: “We are not ready.”

Ms Badenoch was speaking at the London Defence Conference, where she set out her plan to ramp up defence spending.

It came as the US and Iran held the first day of peace talks in Pakistan.

She said President Donald Trump had doled out some uncomfortable home truths — that Britain “cannot properly defend ourselves” without the US.

She said: “It is the culmination of long-standing policy failures which have left our defence capabilities arguably at their weakest in 400 years.

“I don’t need to tell you how this happened.

“Between 1989 and 2022, defence spending fell every year.



“We have grown fat on welfare. Prioritising benefits over bullets.”

The war in Iran exposed our shortcomings — with the UK unable to even send a warship to the region as missiles rained down on our allies and bases, she added.

Ms Badenoch said: “For a proud nation used to stamping its ­influence on the world, Britain’s lack of ­readiness for this war in Iran has been shocking.

“We weren’t just unprepared ­militarily, with no Royal Navy ­warships in the Middle East for the first time in decades. We were strategically unprepared too.”

Blame for this lies with the PM and not our brave Royal Navy, the Tory leader claimed.



She said Sir Keir has been too busy U-turning on benefits and caving to his rebellious backbenchers to prepare for war.

She said: “We have a Government that was politically unprepared for this war, distracted by its own infighting and psychodrama.

“The war in the Gulf must act as a wake-up call. Not for navel ­gazing or finger pointing about who did what, but for action.”

The Government-commissioned strategic defence review, co-authored by General Sir Richard Barrons, was published last year.

It set out the urgent rearming programme needed to make the UK war-ready.



But the Government has still not published the investment plan ­setting out how it will pay for higher defence spending.

Ms Badenoch branded this delay a “national scandal” and added: “Our Government literally doesn’t have a plan.”

Laying out her alternative defence spending blueprint, she promised to cut welfare and Net Zero projects to pay for weapons.

She said: “The next Conservative Government would reinstate the two-child benefit cap and spend that money on defence.

“That will fund the largest net increase in British troops under any Government since the Second World War. We will use the money to recruit 6,000 regular soldiers and 14,000 reservists — as well as paying for their accommodation and equipment.



“And we will reallocate £17billion from Government R&D [research and development work] and Ed Miliband’s disastrous Net Zero ­projects to create a new ­Sovereign Defence Fund.”

In a direct plea to the PM, she said the Tories will put party politics aside and unite with Labour to find cash for defence spending.

She said: “Let’s find the money to rearm. Let’s identify the ­spending cuts.

“And if we reach agreement on a joint plan, Conservatives will ­support those measures in ­Parliament on a three-line whip.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But No10 hit out at the ­Conservative leader’s offer.



A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “Kemi Badenoch sat around the Cabinet table when the Conservatives hollowed-out our Armed Forces. We have announced the biggest uplift in defence spending since the Cold War

“We won’t be taking any advice from her.”

News.title: Construction industry is crying out for young labourers… but Govt policies have priced youngsters out of jobs
News.content:
Shameful waste of Britain’s young

IT IS a national disgrace that a million youngsters are sitting on the scrapheap.

Nearly 13 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds are not in education or employment.



What makes this disaster even worse is that the construction industry is crying out for young labourers.



The Government’s ludicrously ambitious target of building 1.5million new homes by 2029 already looks like falling short by as much as a third.

Building firms need a quarter of a million new workers, like the youngsters we took to sites across the UK this week to get work experience.

So why can’t bosses plug their own gap and take 250k youngsters off the dole at the same time?

Because of the Government’s own ruinous policies of course.



They have priced youngsters out of jobs and tied employers in knots of red tape.

Under Labour’s increased minimum wage, firms simply can’t afford to train young people and the apprentice scheme is a sprawling mess.

This double failure is shameful.

It lets down a generation of youngsters who want to work but are confined to welfare, some for the rest of their lives.



And it is blocking the vital housing programme Britain so desperately needs.

Sir Keir Starmer is keen to trumpet the importance of Labour values.

What value is there in allowing this shambles to continue?

How many chances?

ANYONE who thinks our broken justice system is a recent phenomenon should study the insane case of rapist Neil Trennan.

This monster was first jailed for life in 1990 when he raped a woman after attacking her with a dumb-bell.



Yet in 2002 he was allowed day release, escaped from his supervisor and launched a sexually motivated attack on another woman, receiving a second life sentence.

In any normal system that would be enough to prevent him ever receiving leniency again.

But not in the opinion of the Parole Board, who recommended him for an open prison in 2023.

Astonishingly this fiend, who admitted he was addicted to sexual violence, was then allowed out on unsupervised day release, during which he absconded and tried to rape a third woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge who handed him a third life sentence in February is absolutely right to demand Justice Secretary David Lammy immediately investigate this outrage.



Mr Lammy must identify those responsible for letting this sex beast roam free and kick them out of the justice system.

News.title: Reason Kate keeps her distance from Andrew's daughter Eugenie revealed
News.content:
Reason Kate keeps her distance from Andrew's daughter Eugenie revealed

The two royals are part of the same family, and even went to the same school, but have rarely associated with one another after diverging at a critical point in their youth

View 4 Images Eugenie and Kate rarely cross paths, with the two taking different roles in the Royal Family (Image: Getty Images)

Kate, the Princess of Wales, has been distanced from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's youngest daughter Princess Eugenie - despite having a wealth of reasons to cross paths with her fellow royal.

‌



The pair have rarely been seen together beyond the context of their royal duties, despite having on paper a number of good reasons to socialise. They both went to the same school - the elite Marlborough College - and a clear interest in art. Eugenie is a director at the contemporary art gallery Hauser & Wirth in London, while Kate obtained a master's in Art History at the University of St Andrews, where she met Prince William.

‌



But an expert has revealed that the similarities largely stop there, with the two also typically drawn to different ends of the Royal Family.

‌



New row as locals fume at Kate Middleton's sister after sudden closure on estate READ MORE :

View 4 Images Kate and Eugenie once attended the same school, but their lives have diverged significantly since then (Image: PA)

Speaking to the Daily Mail, royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams said Kate doesn't "have the much in common" with either of the York sisters, who are close with one another. He added that Eugenie also seems to associate more with her cousin, adding: "Eugenie, particularly, seems to be closer to Harry."

The divide may stretch back to their days at Marlborough in Wiltshire, where Kate kept her head down in her studies while Eugenie was once involved in an embarrassing incident.

‌



View 4 Images The Princess of Wales joined the Royal Family in 2011 (Image: FilmMagic)

She was once caught "frolicking naked in the ground" at the plush, £61,000-per-year boarding school following a night of end-of-term drinking in 2008, when she was 18. It was reported at the time that a senior member of staff was awoken by shrieks on the college lawns, who went outside to find the royal and a dozen other students dancing naked in the moonlight.

A staff member told the Sun: "The girls had been drinking, possibly in a local pub, and decided to let their hair down. For some reason they stripped off and started prancing about. It was light-hearted and they were sort of frolicking like nymphs."

‌



View 4 Images Princess Kate has been rarely seen with her two cousins (Image: AP)

"But they got too noisy and staff discovered them. They had to quickly pick up their clothes and hot-foot it inside. She and the others were told they had to go home and only return to take their exams. There were not enough staff on Saturdays and Sundays to supervise them, and they were told they couldn't be trusted to behave."

A source told PA at the time: "It was nothing more than high jinks at the end of term in May. A group of them were reprimanded and that's the end of the matter."

Article continues below

The incident highlighted the clear differences between Kate and Eugenie, with the former of the two joining royal ranks just three years later following a less dramatic time at the college. Both have gone on to hold high-powered professional careers, and have dedicated their lives to charitable causes - but they remain in very different camps of the Royal Family.

News.title: 'I was told I have terminal breast cancer after having baby but still feel lucky'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: 'I was told I have terminal breast cancer after having baby but still feel lucky'

When she was pregnant, Harriet Lawler found a lump under her arm. Now living with incurable cancer, the doting mum shares why she won't give up fighting, for the daughter's sake

View 8 Images Harriet with her husband Joe and their daughter Nellie. Harriet found a lump hours before her baby shower, and weeks before her due date (Image: Supplied)

Having endured chemotherapy, a lumpectomy and 16 rounds of radiotherapy, Harriet Lawler thought she could finally enjoying being a mum again when she was told her cancer was gone. Nine months later and with a holiday in Mauritius with her husband Joe and young daughter Nellie to look forward to, the charity worker was hoping a pain in her arm would prove to be nothing of concern.

‌



But when the results came back last May, Harriet’s worst fears were realised. She says: “I was at work when the surgeon phoned and said there were four nodules on my lungs. I was stunned. I never expected the cancer to have spread to my lungs.” The triple negative breast cancer was now at stage 4. Although treatable, it was incurable. Harriet says: “I left work to call Joe in the car and was sobbing in disbelief. My world stopped when I was told my cancer was incurable, but I still feel lucky to have an amazing husband, the best little girl and wonderful family and friends. I cherish every day.”

‌



Harriet’s cancer journey began as she was getting ready for her baby shower in August 2023. Growing up in Middlesbrough, she and her pals had picked York for the celebration later that day. Harriet, then 33, says: “I was in the shower when I felt a lump in my left armpit. It felt quite big and I had no idea how long it had been there. I’d heard you can get lumpy armpits with hormones in pregnancy. I thought it would be nothing and during my baby shower, I didn’t let it bother me. We had afternoon tea at Betty’s and then cocktails planned. I wasn’t drinking, of course, but I was all dressed up and really looking forward to it.”

‌



8 View 8 Images Harriet, Joe and Nellie - September 2024, just before she found a new lump (Image: Supplied) 8 View 8 Images Harriet and little Nellie, earlier this year (Image: Supplied)

A week later, her GP told Harriet they thought it was hormonal and not to worry, but to come back with any further concerns. Neither she nor Joe, 37, who works in security, were too worried until she found a second lump and was referred to a breast clinic by her doctor.

At 35 weeks pregnant, she was diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer. Harriet says: “It was such a shock. There’s no history of cancer in my family. I’d never checked my breasts for lumps or changes before. I remember briefly seeing something in a magazine about Amy Dowden when I was pregnant, but I didn’t read it properly. I felt for her, but it didn’t feel like something that would ever affect me. When they told me I had to be induced at 36 weeks, I was worried my baby wouldn’t be ready.”

‌



Finally, on October 8, 2023, after a 90-hour induction and a forceps delivery, Nellie was born, at Nottingham City Hospital weighing 7lb. Harriet says: “I had worried before Nellie was born that we might not connect, because of everything going on. But the love was overwhelming. Our bond was instant. I knew I had about a week with her, before my treatment. We really cherished that time.”

8 View 8 Images Harriet, pictured at her baby shower in August 2023 (Image: Supplied) 8 View 8 Images Harriet and Joe on the day Nellie was born (Image: Supplied)

‌



When Nellie was 10 days old, Harriet was back in hospital with five hours to kill before her first chemo. She says: “I set up an email address for Nellie and wrote to her explaining everything that was happening and told her I would document our journey together.” Harriet, head of retail for a charity where she currently works one day a week, reacted to her drugs and had to stay in hospital for three days, leaving Nellie with Joe.

She says: “It gave them some real bonding time. I’m so lucky he’s such a hands-on dad.” After six months of chemo, the lumpectomy and round after round of radiotherapy, Harriet was overjoyed to be told she was cancer free. But in September 2024, three days before a trip to Dublin with friends to celebrate getting the all-clear, Harriet found another lump.

Doctors confirmed her cancer was back and although the lump was removed, the private PET scan would later show that the disease had spread to her lungs. Choosing not to tell anyone else until after the Mauritius holiday so she could process the news, Harriet threw herself into researching ways to stay healthy during the trip. Back home, Harriet emailed her mum Mary, 72, hoping that writing things down would help her to understand the diagnosis. She says: “It was one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to do.”

‌



8 View 8 Images Joe, Harriet and Nellie in Oct 2023, enjoying their time at home before chemo began (Image: Supplied) 8 View 8 Images Harriet, Joe and Nellie in May 2025, the day before finding out that Harriet was stage 4 (Image: Supplied)

Shedding hair, the day before her 35th birthday she went to the hairdressers and had it shaved off. When she saw Nellie, she says: “She ran over, shouted ‘Mummy!’, stroked my head and went back to reading a book.” Currently having chemotherapy two weeks on and one week off, despite numbness and pins and needles in her hands and feet, Harriet says: “I feel fitter and healthier than ever.” She says of Nellie, now two-and-a-half: “She tries to brush my tiny bit of regrown hair.”

‌



Harriet still composes emails for her daughter, saying: “I write about the funny things she does and send her photos, videos and songs we love. I’ve recently told her about my last scan and how there’d been progression, so I’ve changed chemotherapy to try and reduce the tumours in my lungs.”

Harriet also features in Breast Cancer Now’s new TV advert and has raised more than £1,000 for the charity. Almost one million people in the UK are living with, or beyond a breast cancer diagnosis – a figure projected to rise to more than 1.4 million by 2050. The charity has committed to be “Breast Cancer Now until we’re Breast Cancer Never”, reflecting its ambition for everyone with the disease to live and live well by 2050.

View 8 Images "There’s no way I’m giving up. I can’t - for her sake," says Harriet (Image: Supplied)

Article continues below

Due to the amount of lesions in her lungs, Harriet is not eligible for radiotherapy or alternative therapies on the NHS or privately in the UK. Her sister Lucie and niece Lauren launched a GoFundMe page to finance additional treatments for her, costing around £1,500 a month. And Harriet hopes to try cryotherapy at The Hallwang Clinic in Germany that costs from £9,580. She says: “Doctors can’t say exactly how long I have left, but my next big milestone is living to see Nellie start school. There’s no way I’m giving up. I can’t, for her sake.”

News.title: Matthew Perry Ketamine Queen's secret millionaire family and partying after star's death
News.content:
Matthew Perry Ketamine Queen's secret millionaire family and partying after star's death

As Jasveen Sangha gets sentenced to 15 years behind bars for her part in the tragic death of Friends star Matthew Perry, the Mirror takes a look at the 'Ketamine Queen's' glittering lifestyle that concealed a murkey reality

View 6 Images Heiress Jasveen Sangha had a sinister alter-ego, that has lft friends blindsided (Image: INSTAGRAM)

On the surface, Jasveen Sangha lived the life of a glamorous businesswoman, but behind the designer wardrobes and caviar feasts lurked a sinister secret.

‌



Dubbed the 'Ketamine Queen of Los Angeles', Sangha was in fact running a "drug-selling emporium" from her seemingly unremarkable home in North Hollywood. And it was this grubby line of business which resulted in the death of one of the best-loved sit-com stars of all time.

‌



Matthew Perry, famed for playing Chandler Bing in Friends, was just 54-years-old when he was found unresponsive in the hot tub of his LA home on October 28, 2023. His death was ruled an accident from the 'acute effects of ketamine', which had caused him to slip beneath the water and drown.

‌



The tragedy led to an outpouring of grief from fans all across the world, who were sadly all too aware of the TV icon's longstanding issues with drug and alcohol addiction. There was also plenty of outrage directed towards those who had supplied Matthew with drugs.

It was determined that, at the time of the actor's death, British-born Sangha, who plied her trade to "high-end and celebrities", had been his primary supplier. Back in September, having previously denied the charges she faced, the 42-year-old pleaded guilty to five federal counts in Los Angeles, including distributing ketamine resulting in death or bodily injury.

View 6 Images Matthew Perry died on October 28, 2023, aged just 54 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Speaking from jail before she was sentenced to 15 years behind bars this week, Sangha said that she took “full responsibility” for her actions and "the role I played in the events that led to this tragedy." Breaking her silence, Sangha told The Sun: "There are no excuses for what I did. I am deeply sorry for the pain I caused, especially to Matthew's family. Their loss is unimaginable and permanent. I understand that my conduct - operating a drug business and continuing down that path - was reckless, dangerous, and wrong."

Towards the end of his life, Matthew had been receiving off-label ketamine treatments for depression from his usual doctor, but wasn't able to get as much as he wanted. Sangha allegedly provided Matthew with the drug via his friend Erik Fleming, who then gave it to his personal assistant, Kenneth Iwamasa.

In those final days, Iwamasa was administering "at least six shots" of ketamine each day, splurging around £42,000 on the drug. Ahead of sentencing, Matthew's stepmother Debbie Perry called for Sangha to be handed the harshest possible jail sentence, asking: "Please give this heartless woman the maximum prison sentence so she won't be able to hurt other families like ours."

‌



For those who thought they knew Sangha, the realisation that she was living two very different lives simultaneously proved dizzying...

Secret millionaire family

View 6 Images The drug dealer came from enormous wealth

Born in Ilford, east London, Sangha comes from a wealthy Sikh family, and was reportedly "spoilt rotten" by her multimillionaire grandparents during her privileged childhood, the Daily Mail reports. An heiress who stood to inherit a substantial fortune, according to The Times, those close to Sangha have reportedly been left "completely shocked" by her involvement in drug dealing, given the enviable safety net of her rich family.

‌



The daughter of entrepreneur Nilem Singh and Dr Baljeet Singh Chhokar, it initially appeared as though Sangha was set to follow in their footsteps, earning a BA from the University of California, followed by an MBA from Hult Business School. Interior designer Clancy Carter, who has known Sangha since 2008, told the publication: "She has a family that cares for her. She has never been the type of person who needed money. She has property in the UK. She's always travelling and doing fun things with her family. I would never guess she would do something like this at all."

But behind the scenes, the family have navigated some of their own troubles. Sangha's mother and stepfather ran KFC franchises in California. According to the BBC, the couple were sued by the company for more than $50,000 in 2013 for failing to pay royalties for branding use, and Sangha's stepfather declared bankruptcy before the case wrapped up. However, if the family was struggling financially, this certainly wasn't evident in the lifestyle Sangha exhibited.

'Absolutely fabulous' lifestyle

View 6 Images For Sangha, swish holidays and cocktails were a must (Image: instagram)

‌



Sangha's social media pages showcase a life of jetsetting and designer shopping trips, with the Chanel and Louis Vuitton-clad heiress enjoying swish holidays in Mexico and Japan.

Just two weeks after Matthew's death, Sangha was seen sipping lychee martinis at Tokyo's £ 1,500-a-night Mandarin Oriental hotel. A couple of months later, she could be seen sunning herself by the pool with pals in Playa Del Carmen, cocktail in hand.

Right up until her arrest on August 15, 2024, Sangha was still pampering herself with treatments, dying her hair purple the day before she was slapped in cuffs. She also posted a quote from BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, which read: "Cancel my aromatherapy, my psychotherapy, my reflexology, my osteopath, my homoeopath, my naturopath, my crystal reading, my shiatsu, my organic hairdresser. And see if I can be rebirthed next Thursday afternoon."

‌



Much like image-conscious characters Patsy and Eddie, Sangha spared no expense when it came to trying out treatments, recuperating after parties with IV drips and 'sound healing' sessions. And when it came to parties, she also didn't hold back. Sangha, who socialised with the likes of Charlie Sheen, threw her 41st birthday at a trendy West Hollywood bar, while her '70s-themed 40th saw her decked in sequins, posing beside a plush Mercedes.

Star-studded career

View 6 Images Schmoozing at red carpet events was all part of Sangha's brand (Image: Jojo Korsh/BFA.com/REX/Shutterstock)

Sangha concealed her drug-dealing activities behind a sparkling career, which saw her mingle with actors on the red carpet. One pal told the Daily Mail that she worked in marketing and event planning for the rich and famous, and had previously attended Golden Globes and Oscars events. Her social media bio paints the criminal as a curator of art, events and music, keeping her less palatable activities out of view.

‌



For Kayti Edwards, who dated Matthew in 2006 before becoming his assistant, Sangha's reported presence at glittering events such as the Oscars was a sign of how widespread drug use is in Hollywood. Kayti revealed: 'I don't think she had a purse full of drugs at the Oscars… I think she was treating it like a networking party. When you hang around all these powerful people with money, opportunity always presents itself. She would have definitely made some contacts there."

According to The Sun, the MBA grad also owned businesses. This included nail salon Stiletto Nail Bar, located in the stylish LA neighbourhood of Studio City, which reportedly opened in 2015, only to close just two years later. Behind the scenes lay a darker empire. Officers who raided Sangha's home uncovered what they called a “drug-selling emporium”, described as the hub of a vast operation dealing in methamphetamine, cocaine, Xanax and ketamine.

Friends' shock

View 6 Images Officers who raided Sangha's home uncovered what they called a 'drug-selling emporium' (Image: Jonathan Buckmaster)

‌



In December 2025, one of Sangha's longtime friends, Tony Marquez, spoke out in the BBC documentary Matthew Perry and the Ketamine Queen, expressing shock over the businesswoman's "double life". Mere weeks before Matthew's death, Tony, who'd known Sangha since the 2010s, spoke with her over the phone, not realising the sinister turn her life had taken.

Tony, who had moved in the same fashionable social circles as Sangha and even met her family, claimed: "She never hinted that she was in deep water." He recalled: "She always had money. She travelled all over by private jet, and did that way before everything blew up."

Meanwhile, her old university pal Jash Negandhi told the BBC he'd been completely blindsided by the revelations, and says his former classmates never discussed any involvement in drugs. He shared: "She was very much into the dance music scene. She loved to dance and have a good time. I knew nothing. Absolutely nothing."

Article continues below

*Frank offers confidential advice about drugs and addiction (email frank@talktofrank.com, message 82111 or call 0300 123 6600) or the NHS has information about getting help.

News.title: Rachel Reeves issues warning on cost of Iran war and teases support package
News.content:
Rachel Reeves issues warning on cost of Iran war and teases support package

Chancellor Rachel Reeves admitted the scale of the costs of the Iran war are not yet known but repeated her vow to 'provide support for those who need it most' in the UK

View 2 Images Rachel Reeves has warned “the war in Iran will come at a cost to British families and businesses” (Image: PA)

Rachel Reeves has warned “the war in Iran will come at a cost to British families and businesses”. The Chancellor said a two-week US-Iran ceasefire is the "best protection" for household bills but acknowledged that rising prices are already being felt here at home. She admitted the scale of the costs are not yet known but repeated her vow to "provide support for those who need it most".

‌



Ms Reeves said she will this week set out the "principles" for how the Government will support business in the coming months and the "next phase" of boosting Britain's competitiveness.

‌



Writing in The Times, Ms Reeves said: “I am going to be straight with people though that the war in Iran will come at a cost to British families and business.

‌



“These are not costs I wanted, but they are costs we will have to respond to. As Chancellor, I have vowed that my economic approach to this crisis will be both responsive to a changing world and responsible in the national interest.

UK is rewriting war response for the first time in 50 years — from rationing to hospitals READ MORE :

View 2 Images Health Secretary Wes Streeting said it was 'disappointing' there had not been a breakthrough in Iran peace talks (Image: PA)

“We don’t yet know the full scale of those costs, but the immediate priority must be to ensure that the ceasefire holds. “That is the best protection we have against higher costs at home and at the IMF meetings in Washington this week I will be working with allies on the action we can take to guarantee freedom of navigation, including the Strait of Hormuz, to keep energy supplies moving again. “But I know rising prices are being felt now. So, we are taking action to keep costs down for families and provide support for those who need it most.”

‌



Addressing the pressure on businesses, Ms Reeves added: “I know that rising energy bills are not only felt by households. They are felt by business too, including the UK’s manufacturing sector that has faced uncompetitive energy prices for too long.

“So later this week I will be setting out the next phase of our plans to boost Britain’s competitiveness. I will also set out the principles that will guide how we support businesses in the months ahead.”

said that although the scale of the costs were not known, the Government is committed to providing support to those who need it.

‌



Her comments come after Keir Starmer last week admitted he was "fed up" with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin ’s actions pushing up household bills in the UK. He has told the US President about the need for a “practical plan” to get ships going through the area amid suggestions Iran wants to charge vessels for passage.

The PM has been leading European efforts to try to re-open the Tehran-blockaded Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route that transports around a fifth of the world's oil.

A US-Iran ceasefire attempting to reopen the Strait has faced cracks since being agreed earlier this week. Gas prices have risen sharply during the ongoing closure of the Strait.

‌



Britain will host further talks on reopening the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping lane with a coalition of countries next week. The meeting will continue the Government’s efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait.

US vice president JD Vance is in Pakistan for peace talks with Iran, although a 21-hour session ended without a deal being reached in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Health Secretary Wes Streeting said it was "disappointing" there had not been a breakthrough in talks in Islamabad, Pakistan's capital. On Sunday morning, he told Sky News: "It's obviously disappointing that we haven't yet seen a breakthrough in negotiations and an end to this war in Iran. That is a sustainable one. But as ever in diplomacy, you're failing until you succeed.

Article continues below

"So while these talks may not have ended in success, that doesn't mean there isn't merit in continuing to try. And clearly, when you look at the impact of the war in Iran on this country, on other countries around the world who have no part in this war, it is in all of our interests for there to be a breakthrough and an end to this war."

Elsewhere, Mr Streeting accused Mr Trump of saying some "incendiary, provocative, outrageous things on social media". He said: "I think we've all come to learn that you judge President Trump through what he does, not just what he says. And ultimately, the only way in which we're going to clear this situation up is to reach agreement with Iran, one that puts nuclear weapons beyond its ambitions and reach."

News.title: Brit survivors of La Gomera bus tragedy compare crash scene to 'horror movie'
News.content:
Brit survivors of La Gomera bus tragedy compare crash scene to 'horror movie'

Investigators are continuing to probe whether a brake problem caused the crash, which killed a 77-year-old man and left more than 20 Brits, including three children, shaken and injured

View 5 Images The bus crashed off a mountain pass on the Spanish Island of La Gomera on Friday afternoon (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

Survivors of the La Gomera bus tragedy that killed a British pensioner and injured 27 others have described the crash as "like something out of a horror movie".

‌



All of the victims who have been released from hospital, including three children, are now being supported by consular officials and experts at the island's Bancal Hotel & Spa. One British couple staying there, who did not want to be named, have described the crash in the Canary Islands "like something out of a horror movie".

‌



They said they felt "time slowed down" and they "went head over heels twice". They also added luckily they had their seat belts on, but when the bus stopped they were left hanging from their seats.

‌



View 5 Images Some 28 people, all Brits except the driver, were onboard at the time. The driver and five Brits were still in hospital on Saturday afternoon (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

Widow of Brit killed in Canary Island bus crash among 27 hospitalised READ MORE :

The elderly couple reportedly said they felt like they were the lucky ones because they were walking away with just bruises. Other survivors have described the crash as "traumatising and terrifying."

Their testimony came after we told how the heartbroken widow of the 77-year-old Brit killed in the crash only discovered her husband had died when told by doctors. The woman, thought to have been sitting next to him, was taken to a nearby hospital, where she asked medics: “Where is my husband?”

‌



The man died instantly when the vehicle came off the GM-2 near a bend plunged 50ft into rocks on Friday afternoon. Guacimara Barrera, of La Gomera’s Hospital Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, said: “The wife was not aware of this at the scene and when she came to the hospital. She was in shock, and we were very sensitive in [informing her].”

His wife was moved to the Bancal Hotel after leaving hospital, where she is now being cared for. Ms Barrera said: “We decided the best place she could be was with everyone because they are doing therapies to overcome the shock of the accident.”

View 5 Images The bus was left partly crumpled with all of its windows smashed following the crash (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

‌



Guardia Civil traffic officers spent about 90 minutes at the four-star hotel on Saturday gathering witness testimony. Juan Luis Navarro, the Spanish central government’s representative on the island, said: “The hypothesis is that there was a mechanical problem, possibly with the brakes. But we are not sure about that because police must also take declarations from the other people inside the bus.

“They are really emotionally affected, so it will be possibly [Saturday and Sunday] I think they will take more declarations.” Mr Navarro said the survivors were taken to the Bancal Hotel & Spa as they did not want to return to their previous hotel high up in the hills.

To get there, they would have had to travel past the scene of Friday’s tragedy, including the wreckage of the bus, which fell an estimated 50ft below the road. It had been travelling downhill towards the airport at around 1.15pm on Friday when the driver, said to be aged in his 50s, reportedly realised he had a problem with his brakes.

‌



He is said to have tried to pull intoa side road and then a gravel track ina bid to bring the vehicle to a natural stop. But, tragically, the vehicle, owned by La Gomera Tours, collided with a Toyoya pick-up truck and then carried on towards the unfenced edge before plunging down into rocks and foliage.

View 5 Images A Toyota pick-up truck was damaged in the horrifying incident (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

Some 28 people were onboard at the time. Six, including five Brits, were still in hospital on Saturday afternoon. Three, including a married couple, were being treated at Nuestra Señora, just minutes from the crash site. The three more seriously injured, including the driver, were airlifted to the neighbouring island of Tenerife on Friday for treatment.

‌



Speaking of three people still inthe Nuestra Señora, including at least one person in their 70s, Mr Navarro said: “I think they are getting better.“ There will be more medical testsjust to know how they are exactly.“ Once they see the evolution, the doctors will decide what other tests must be conducted.”

Less than 12 months ago there wasa similar crash on the GM-2 road,which connects the capital San Sebastian with the rest of the mountainous island. In May, a 73-year-old Spanishwoman died and 11 others were injured when a bus overturned on astraight stretch of the road and tumbled down a hill.

View 5 Images Police are continuing to probe the cause of the crash (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

Article continues below

La Gomera Tours has said all of itsvehicles are “up to date” with inspections and it was not aware of any incident or complaint from their drivers regarding that stretch of road. A representative has told Spanish media the driver was a local man, experienced and passed the crash spot “virtually every day”.

A spokeswoman for tour operator The Holiday Property Bond said: “Our immediate focus is on the safety and wellbeing of everyone affected. We recognise this is an extremely distressing situation for those involved, as well as for their families and loved ones, and our thoughts are with them at this difficult time.”

Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “My thoughts are with those affected by the tragic incident involving a bus carrying British holidaymakers in the Canary Islands.”

News.title: Omeprazole patients with acid reflux told 'red flag issue' by NHS GP and BBC star
News.content:
Omeprazole patients with acid reflux told 'red flag issue' by NHS GP and BBC star

Dr Punam Krishan explained everything to people taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole for heartburn, acid reflux, and indigestion

View 3 Images The NHS GP urges anyone taking PPIs to get regular check-ups to avoid long-term risks and symptoms (Image: Getty)

BBC Morning Live's Dr Punam Krishan shared important guidance for anyone using proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole, for conditions including heartburn, acid reflux, and indigestion. In the UK, one in four adults suffers from acid reflux, with many people experiencing it at some stage in their lives, particularly following large meals.

‌



Those who experience it regularly may be prescribed PPIs like omeprazole to help manage symptoms. However, Dr Punam outlined why people using the medication need to exercise caution, especially if they're taking it long-term, and emphasised the need for routine medical reviews.

‌



Dr Punam is a serving NHS GP and acts as the resident doctor on BBC's Morning Live. She is also a media medic, health broadcaster, and the author of children's books.

‌



Addressing the BBC Morning Live presenters, Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton, in a previous episode of the show, the health professional began by explaining what acid reflux is. She said: "Acid reflux is all about what happens in your stomach. So we all have acid in our stomach and it has a very important role. The role of that is to break down and digest the food. Now, at the top of the stomach, we have a little valve, a sphincter, and it acts like a trapdoor.

"And its job is to basically seal the contents so the acid is not essentially tracking back up the food pipe, your oesophagus. However, if that sphincter, that valve, becomes too loose, it can become very relaxed by things like heavy meals. If you've had alcohol, if you lie down straight after having a heavy meal, that can actually mean that that acid from the stomach can end up creeping back up the food pipe and cause that heavy pressured burning sensation that people get."

‌



Presenter Gethin enquired: "What about the most common ways to treat it then?" Dr Punam explained: "So there are lots of different things that we can do. If, of course, you're having it just every now and then, then lots of people do get antacids or basically medications like alginates. Examples of that include Gaviscon. And these basically help to just kind of neutralise the acid. They're very effective and you can just use them as and when needed."

"However, if the discomfort is persistent, we often prescribe proton pump inhibitors, PPIs for short. Examples of these are omeprazole, lansoprazole. And these are incredible and have really transformed the way that we treat acid reflux. They essentially help to treat the acid production at the source."

Issuing a cautionary note to anyone taking PPIs, the NHS GP said: "Essentially these medications aren't there to be used unnecessarily or for a long period of time. They do require us to review them. And that's because if used over a long period of time, they can slightly increase your risk of things like low magnesium, low vitamin B12, but also increase the risk of gut infections, particularly Clostridioides difficile. We call that C. diff for short."

‌



View 3 Images Dr Punam explains what’s behind the concern, the warning signs to watch out for, and how to manage symptoms safely (Image: BBC Morning Live)

She stressed the significance of routine check-ups for those taking PPIs over an extended period. Dr Punam continued: "Now, we have this bacteria in our bowel, you and I, we all have it, and it lives in balance. However, medications like PPIs can tip that balance." Sharing a 'red flag' issue to be aware of, she added: "And if you get overgrowth of this bacterium, it can cause persistent diarrhoea. That is a red flag.

"So you do need to speak to your doctor if that is an issue and you suddenly start developing diarrhoea. Or if you've got a change in bowel habit, we always say check in with your doctor. Just make sure that you are getting those reviews with your GP."

‌



Helen said: "I guess the trouble is if it works, you stick with it, don't you?" Dr Punam replied: "Yeah, it is." Gethin said: "But you don't even know how long you're taking it for in the end, are you?" Dr Punam told him: "Well, that's just it. Sometimes you can just be taking it, and the problem is resolved, but you're just taking the medication. So do go in for your regular reviews."

How frequently should people taking PPIs visit their GP?

If you are taking omeprazole without a prescription, do not take it for longer than two weeks. You should see a doctor if:

Your symptoms do not improve after 14 days.

Your symptoms worsen.

Your symptoms return sooner than four months after finishing treatment.

You experience alarming symptoms like difficulty swallowing, bloody vomit, or black stools.

‌



If your GP has prescribed omeprazole for long-term use, they should keep a close eye on you on a regular basis. Your doctor should establish a schedule for follow-up appointments based on your individual health needs and risk factors, for instance, every six to 12 months. If your GP recommends omeprazole for over a year, it's absolutely essential to attend regular check-ups to minimise the likelihood of experiencing long-term side effects.

View 3 Images Long term use of PPIs without regular check ups can lead to various serious health complications

What warning signs should you be watching for?

Indicators of low magnesium include muscle cramps, fatigue, and an irregular heartbeat, as well as less obvious symptoms such as loss of appetite, nausea, and general weakness. More serious deficiencies can result in numbness, tingling, personality changes, seizures, and abnormal heart rhythms.

‌



Indicators of low vitamin B12 include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and a sore or swollen red tongue. Further symptoms can include neurological issues such as pins and needles, difficulty with balance, and memory problems, as well as shortness of breath, heart palpitations, and digestive complaints.

Symptoms of a C. diff gut infection include watery diarrhoea, stomach cramps and pain, a high temperature (fever), nausea, loss of appetite, and dehydration. In severe cases, potentially life-threatening complications can develop, such as serious inflammation of the intestines.

What tests are available to check for these conditions?

Helen questioned: "What if you want to do something without medication? Can you ease the symptoms without taking any meds?" The NHS GP responded: "So if you have got symptoms that have not settled despite you trying to manage them, then it is important to check in with your GP because we would want to investigate that further.

‌



"Ultimately, you want to find out what is the root cause of this and is it something more serious? We would do tests like checking for a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori, which increases the production of acid. We may refer you for a gastroscopy. This is a camera test that goes into the stomach to see is there any inflammation, any ulcers, anything more serious."

Dr Punam then moved on to reveal details of a groundbreaking new test. "There is a really exciting pilot at the moment that is being tried out by the NHS across pharmacies in England," she explained.

"And it is to try to identify any early changes that could increase your risk of oesophageal cancer. It's called the sponge on a string test. And it involves putting a tiny capsule that's attached to a thread down through the mouth into the stomach. It opens up like a tiny little sponge. It takes little cells from the stomach and the lining of your food pipe, your oesophagus. We pull it back out, and essentially, it's easy if any cellular changes have happened. This is fantastic. If it is successful and it gets rolled out, we could pick up changes much earlier on."

‌



What other options are available beyond medication?

Dr Punam said: "At the end of the day, medications are great, but there's lots of things that we can do every day in our lifestyles that make a massive, massive difference. The first thing is if you are struggling with heartburn, indigestion, acid reflux, then eat smaller portions.

"If you eat big, heavy meals, you can actually put a lot of pressure on your stomach. Again, we're going back to that valve, which can become a bit lax and cause acid to track up. Avoid lying down after a meal for at least three to four hours. When we lie flat, the sphincter relaxes, and acid can return to the oesophagus.

Article continues below

"If you have symptoms, prop up your pillows so your chest is slightly higher than your waist, so you're just slouched up a little bit. Again, avoid lying flat. It really, really works a treat. Don't wear tight clothes. We all want to loosen that button on your jeans after a meal, but actually just get into looser clothing because tight clothes can actually put a lot of pressure on your stomach as well.

"Gentle teas like chamomile work really well. Ginger tea is fantastic. Chamomile works really well, ginger tea is fantastic. A lot of people turn to mint. Now mint is great if you've got IBS or tummy cramps, but actually for reflux it can make the problem worse. So stick to ginger tea or chamomile tea.

"Avoid certain foods as well. Knowing your triggers. So keep a diary. I'm a big one for diaries. Look at when you get your symptoms, what have you had or done that day that could have exacerbated them. Taking them into your doctor is a real help to us. And that and also managing your weight. I think that goes without saying can make a big difference."

News.title: DWP benefits alert over payments for people with this health condition
News.content:
DWP benefits alert over payments for people with this health condition

MPs discussed proposals to improve access to DWP benefits

View Image You may want to check if you can claim more DWP benefits (Image: Getty)

MPs have spoken about proposals to enhance access to DWP benefits. People may want to do a quick check to see if they can claim any more Government support, in light of the discussion.

‌



Various payments are available from the DWP, including Universal Credit and PIP (Personal Independence Payment) for those of working age, or Pension Credit and Attendance Allowance for those of state pension age. The Treasury Committee recently consulted with policy advocates about efforts to expand access to the benefits system. Discussions centred on the Government's Financial Inclusion Strategy, a policy aimed at boosting financial engagement and awareness of the support available to people.

‌



Helen Undy, chief executive of the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute, which was founded by financial journalist Martin Lewis, highlighted a crucial omission from the strategy. She said: "The bit that could have gone in this strategy that is missing is around how you address the £24billion a year of unclaimed benefits-that figure is from Policy in Practice."

‌



State Pensioners to face major tax change

Financially excluded

She added: "We should be talking about how we increase access to income maximisation support for people who are financially excluded and who are living on low incomes. I would like to have seen that in the section of the strategy that talks about debt advice."

She continued by noting that certain groups in particular could benefit from more assistance, to ensure they receive all the income they're entitled to through the benefits system. Ms Undy urged: "Our research suggests that, particularly for people with more complex needs, like mental health problems, having access to an individual-face to face, ideally, or over the telephone-who can give them income maximisation support can be transformational.

‌



"That is a key thing that I think is missing in the strategy, but that we could still go further on. I would like to see more on that."

There are several benefit calculator tools available to help you determine if you're eligible for additional benefits. For instance, there is one available on the Turn2us website.

State pension check

Another benefit worth exploring is your state pension entitlement. The full new state pension currently provides £241.30 weekly.

‌



Payments increased by 4.8 per cent in April due to the triple lock. The policy ensures the state pension rises each April in line with the higher of 2.5 per cent, the rise in average earnings, or inflation.

Your entitlement is built up through your National Insurance (NI) payments. Typically, you require 35 years of NI contributions to receive the full amount.

People can check their projected amount using the state pension forecast tool on the Government website. This tool also indicates whether you can boost your entitlement by voluntarily purchasing more NI contributions.

Article continues below

It's crucial to first check that buying extra contributions will genuinely increase your entitlement before paying for them, as this may not be the case.

News.title: Darlington cop killed pensioner racing through red light on 999 call to baby
News.content:
Darlington cop killed pensioner racing through red light on 999 call to baby

PC Mark Roberts was jailed for speeding through a red light while responding to a 999 call where he smashed into an elderly couple and killed a 74-year-old woman

View 2 Images PC Mark Roberts has been jailed (Image: PA)

A police officer who raced through the streets in response to a call about a choking baby has been jailed after his car crashed into a motorbike and killed a woman.

‌



PC Mark Roberts of Northumbria Police was responding to the grade-one emergency call when his marked car smashed into an elderly couple, Ronald and Muriel Pinkney, as they rode their motorbike in Gateshead, north East, on July 8, 2022.

‌



A court heard how Roberts, from Darlington, was driving at 43mph on the 30mph stretch of road near the MetroCentre. As he approached the lights, he was driving around 25mph when his car crashed into the couple, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

‌



Mrs Pinkney, 74, tragically suffered fatal injuries to her head and neck in the horror smash which occurred on a 30mph stretch of road near the MetroCentre. Mr Pinkney also sustained injuries, including a bleed on the brain and several fractures.

The cop has since been prosecuted and convicted of of causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious injury by dangerous driving, Birmingham Live reports, despite a plea from the couple's daughter not to send him to prison.

Roberts was arrested after the collision and answered 'no comment' to questions during his police interview but provided a prepared statement.

‌



In it, he said the ambulance service had requested assistance about a choking five-week-old baby, which indicated paramedics did not believe they could get to the patient before police.

Roberts said he took his marked vehicle from Whickham police station, activated his blue lights and sirens, changing the tone of the alert at times, as he made his way through traffic and red lights.

View 2 Images The cop said he was 'heartbroken' by the tragedy (Image: PA)

‌



Moments before the collision, the officer saw a white van make an emergency stop. He said: "I couldn't see anything else before travelling towards the junction. The next thing I recall is there was a bang and both airbags deployed and I hit the windscreen, which knocked me out for a few seconds."

He he then saw two people on the ground with crash helmets on. Roberts blacked out again and was treated in an ambulance and then taken to hospital. He said: "I believe this was a tragic accident."

Jurors were told Northumbria Police's roadcraft guidance stated that risk taking, even in a 'noble cause', was not justified. In mitigation, the court heard Roberts was 'heartbroken' by the ordeal.

‌



The court was told he had led a 'remarkable life of public service', joining the police after an Army career which saw him serve in Yugoslavia, Afghanistan and Iraq.

He was jailed for two years and three months at Teesside Crown Court on Tuesday (April 7).

Passing sentence, Judge Francis Laird KC, said: "In my judgement only a custodial sentence can be justified for these offences."

‌



The judge told Roberts that he was entitled to use exemptions from the speed limit and the ban on driving through red lights but that 'these exemptions must be exercised cautiously and appropriately'.

"Your speed as you approached the junction was too high," the judge said. "You observed the junction was clear and you simply chose to drive through without stopping or at least reducing your speed to a point where you could stop should another motorist enter the junction."

He went on to say: "The evidence suggests Ronald and Muriel Pinkney were visible to you when you approached the junction, however you were so focused on getting to your destination you failed to notice them."

‌



Roberts was also banned from driving for five years and one month.

The couple's daughter, Dawn Hunter-Pinkney, said in a statement that the family 'don't blame the officer for what happened'.

She said: "For a long time we were angry but the more we hear about why the officer was driving the way he was, the more we understand." She went on to say: "We don't want him to go to prison for doing his job.

‌



"We do accept this is a very tragic accident with a very tragic outcome, but sending the officer to prison won't bring mam back."

Ms Hunter-Pinkney said her parents had been inseparable and her dad had been 'devastated' by his wife's death, going from doing everything with her to 'doing almost nothing'.

She said: "My dad used to be very active and fit, now he rarely leaves the house."

Article continues below

Roberts has been suspended by the force. Andy Hill, assistant chief constable of Northumbria Police, said: "I reiterate my previous comments in recognising that no words will make the pain of Mr Pinkney, his family and anyone impacted by this tragic incident, any easier.

"On behalf of Northumbria Police, I wish to express my sincere condolences for your loss and our thoughts very much continue to be with you at this time." He added: "Each and every day we respond to emergencies and thankfully tragedies of this nature are extremely rare.

"Officers are highly trained and supported to help ensure they keep both themselves and the public safe. Regrettably, on this occasion the standard of driving fell short of what it is expected which has led to the most devastating of outcomes."

News.title: I Am Maximus wins Grand National for trainer Mullins
News.content:
I Am Maximus became the first horse since Red Rum in 1977 to regain the Grand National as trainer Willie Mullins celebrated his third consecutive victory in the race at Aintree.

The 2024 winner and last year's runner-up came into the race as the 9-2 favourite and backed that up by finishing ahead of Iroko, Jordans and Johnnywho.

It made Irishman Mullins, who won the race for a fourth time in total, the first trainer since Vincent O'Brien between 1953 and 1955 to win in three successive years.

The feat means that JP McManus is now the leading owner in the history of the race with four wins - backing up the victories of Don't Push It in 2010, Minella Times in 2021 and I Am Maximus in 2024.

McManus could also boast owning three of the top four in Saturday's showpiece race, with only Jordans not in his stable.

Red Rum's second and third victories came in 1974 and 1977, and I Am Maximus is the first horse to have won the race in non-consecutive years since.

Further history for I Am Maximus was made by him, with a handicap of 11st 12lbs, becoming the first top weight to win since Red Rum carried 12 stone to victory in 1974.

Jockey Paul Townend said he felt "privileged" to be riding I Am Maximus.

He told ITV: "He's tough. He's a really, really good horse, and although Grangeclare West and Nick Rockett looked good in training, this lad wasn't telling me not to ride him.

"He is so good and has such an engine. He will gallop to the end of the world for you. I am really privileged. What a horse.

"Grand Nationals and Gold Cups are the pinnacle of the sport and I have them both."

News.title: Jack Whitehall jokes he booked Scott Mills for his wedding in SNL monologue
News.content:
Jack Whitehall joked about former BBC Radio 2 DJ Scott Mills during his Saturday Night Live UK monologue last night (11 April).

The actor and comedian, 37, who is known for his risque sense of humour, began speaking about his upcoming wedding to Roxy Horner and the "out of control" cost of the nuptials.

Mills was sacked by the BBC shortly before it emerged the Metropolitan Police launched an investigation into him in 2016 over allegations of serious sexual offences involving a teenage boy under 16 between 1997 and 2000.

The 53-year-old released a statement through his lawyers saying he had been the subject of “rumour and speculation” since he was fired, and that he “co-operated fully” with the police investigation into allegations of a historical sexual offence.

Ben Coyle-Larner, aka the musician Loyle Carner, has opened up about his foray into acting, while speaking at the launch of BBC One’s eight-part crime drama series, Mint, coming out at the end of April.

“I was just really nervous, you know? I was pretty scared,” he admitted, as he discussed making the transition after 12 years in music.

Mint tells the story of Shannon (Emma Laird), a daughter born into a Scottish crime family, who is waiting for romance to sweep her off her feet. Carner, credited here as Ben Coyle-Larner, makes his acting debut as Arran, a young man returning from London as the prodigal son of a rival crime family.

open image in gallery Ben Coyle-Larner makes his acting debut in this series, which co-stars Emma Laird ( BBC )

Arran is Shannon’s love interest in this Romeo and Juliet style tale, with the two characters embarking on a complex relationship full of highs and lows.

Speaking at the British Film Insititute’s (BFI) screening of the first two episodes on Thursday night (9 April), Coyle-Larner recalled a conversation with director, Charlotte Regan, on how to channel his nerves into positivity and excitement.

“I remember at the start I said to [Regan], ‘I should do prep, actors do prep, I don’t know what prep is. What should I do?’

“She said, ‘Honestly, just how you feel now, how nervous you are and how everything is new and exciting to you – just hold onto that because it’s rare.”

The three-time Brit nominee acknowledged that it felt “weird to be a true rookie” at something after spending most of his life developing his music career, “being 31 and coming into something brand new”.

Coyle-Larner grew up and studied in south London before earning a scholarship to attend the Brit School for Performing Arts and Technology. He later turned to rapping, releasing his first EP at the age of 19, titled, A Little Late. Coyle-Larner began to use music as an outlet to explore everything from mental health struggles to his experiences with fatherhood.

This is not technically Coyle-Larner’s acting debut. He had a small role as a young hunter in the 2008 action movie 10,000 BC – but it’s not something he’s keen to dwell on. When the subject came up, he glanced down, visibly embarrassed, and asked jokingly, “not to bring that up!”

The hip-hop musician told the audience that he came to learn that, in some ways, acting is not too different to music after all.

“It’s kind of the same, but different,” he said. “[Both are] a space to create – this was just like trying to learn how to use a different part of me to do the same thing, to tell a story.”

open image in gallery Coyle-Larner said he was ‘really nervous’ to star in ‘Mint’ ( BBC )

Coyle-Larner added that, while he was apprehensive about his first big acting role, there was also a bizarre sense of “relief” he felt in the production of Mint.

“I’m used to being too much in control of what I release and what I share,” he told the BFI audience. He explained that when he was acting, he didn’t feel the need to be “f***ing stressing about it”, he added with a laugh.

He ultimately felt that the novelty of the experience for him actually translated into something exciting for everyone else on set as well.

“For everything to be magic for me, I think it was useful to everyone else because I think it’s so easy to get used to the thing you do for your job. And because it was brand new to me, I think it became brand new for everyone. That’s what I hope I brought,” Coyle-Larner said, cheekily adding: “And a lot of snacks as well.”

All episodes of Mint will be available on BBC iPlayer from 6am on Monday 20th April, with the series airing on BBC One from 9pm the same night.
